abstract: Genome function is regulated temporally and tissue-specifically through coordinated interplay between epigenetic modifications and genomic elements, however, the extent to which chromatin conformation shapes or is shaped by epigenetic programming and transcriptional activity in vivo, remains largely unresolved. Through analysis of the well-characterised Dlk1-Dio3 imprinted domain, we have identified tissue and parent-of-origin specific conformations and taken a genetic approach to determine the hierarchical relationships between conformation, epigenetic state and transcription. Parental-origin specific topological domains identified in fetal brain are dependent on the germline-derived imprinting control region. In the absence of specific CTCF binding at a secondary imprinting control element, the parental origin-specific CTCF-mediated conformation can be disrupted without a change to domain-wide imprinting, transcription or epigenetic state. These findings indicate that, in this developmental context, conformation can be decoupled from transcription and that each can be independently governed by a hierarchy of epigenetically controlled regulatory features initiated in the germline.
